headline: A rare moth set a record in Essex. The plan took 21 years.
summary: Fisher's estuarine moth was spotted 111 times this year at Abbotts Hall, a reserve near Colchester. That is a record. It lives on one rare plant, hog's fennel, and rising seas have hurt the plant. Essex Wildlife Trust planted the fennel there in 2005 and added moth eggs five years later. It now calls the population self-sustaining.

cover_question.q: Why spend 21 years on one moth?

cover_answer: It lives on one rare plant, and rising seas hurt that plant.
table_question: Is a small win still a win if the big problem hasn't moved?

5-7.script: In England this year, people counted a rare gold-brown moth 111 times, more than ever before. The moth can only live near one special plant, so 21 years ago some grown-ups planted that plant and, five years later, brought the moth's eggs. Twenty-one years is three of your whole life. It worked, and the moths are staying.
5-7.why: Counting is a thing they do. 111 moths and a 21-year wait are numbers they can hold, and the wait is measured in their own life.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, and a moth on the English coast is a long way off. The script hands them two numbers instead, 111 and 21 years, and makes the years three of their own life, which is a size they can feel. Expect 'can we plant one?' You can plant something. Say yes to that and skip the fennel.

8-12.script: This moth lives on one rare plant, hog's fennel, and rising seas have hurt it. So in 2005 Essex Wildlife Trust planted the fennel at Abbotts Hall, then brought moth eggs five years later. Plant first, moth second, like filling the feeder before you expect birds. This year the count hit 111, a record.
8-12.why: Plant, eggs, count is a chain in order, and they can follow it, even one that took five years to show.
8-12.why_long: A ten-year-old is working out cause and effect, and this story is a chain: the sea hurt the plant, the plant went in first, the eggs came five years later, the count climbed. The feeder is a mechanism they know. Expect 'what if the sea keeps rising?' Honest answer: fennel is in at three more reserves, and nobody knows.

13-17.script: Why spend 21 years on one moth? Essex Wildlife Trust planted a rare plant in 2005, added moth eggs in 2010, and counted 111 Fisher's estuarine moths this year, a record. Second: the sea that threatens the plant is still rising, so is 111 moths at one reserve a win or a holding action?
13-17.why: A record and a rising sea. Give them both; at fifteen they can hold a win and a threat at once.
13-17.why_long: A fifteen-year-old can hold two true things at once: 111 moths is a record, and the sea that threatens the plant is still rising. The script hands them both and asks which word fits, win or holding action. Expect 'why this moth and not something bigger?' Say you don't know how the trust chose, and ask what they would have picked.

5-7.a: Not from here. It lives in grass on the coast of England. It is gold-brown with light and dark spots.

8-12.q: Why did they plant the plant first?
8-12.a: The moth can't live without hog's fennel. Plant in 2005, eggs in 2010.
For this moth, yes. Last year was the first time it passed 100.

13-17.q: Why spend 21 years on one moth?
13-17.a: One rare plant, hurt by rising seas, and a method the trust says worked.

13-17.q: Does the moth matter, or just the method?
13-17.a: The trust's own line is about the method. The moths are the proof.
